raw_case_text: In February 2016, a male in his 40s was admitted to the neurology department of a hospital in Paramaribo, Suriname, because of muscle weakness in the legs, which started 7 days prior to admission. At presentation in the hospital, the patient was unable to walk without help. Two weeks before muscle weakness started he visited the hospital because of urinary retention. Acute myelitis and a cauda syndrome were excluded with an MRI-scan, which showed no abnormalities. The week before muscle weakness started he had an influenza-like syndrome and had a short episode of diplopia. At first physical examination after admission, muscle weakness was observed in predominantly the legs (MRC score 4). Areflexia in both legs and arms was noted. The patient complained of paresthesias and pain in the legs but did not have a sensory level or other signs of myelum involvement. A lumbar puncture was performed 2 days after admission, and a high protein level was found in the CSF (4.4 g/L) while the cell count was slightly increased (32.7 x 106/L). A urine sample, taken at day two after admission, was tested positive for ZIKV RNA with a Ct-value of 35.7. Four days after admission his muscle power improved (MCR score arms 5, legs; proximal 5, distal 4), while the areflexia in arms and legs persisted. Because of the little availability of IVIg in Suriname and because PE is not possible in Suriname, the patient did not received immunotherapy. A motor NCS, performed 15 days after the start of muscle weakness, showed severe decreased NCV and a prolonged DML in all tested nerves. The CMAP was decreased in predominantly the legs (see Table S2 in Supplementary Material). These results were consistent with the demyelinating subtype of GBS. At discharge, 7 days after admission, he was still unable to walk without help due to muscle weakness in the legs. Four months after hospital discharge he was able to walk a few steps without assistance, but he still could not live independently or return to work.

subjective.chief_complaint: Male in his 40s presenting with progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness for 7 days, resulting in inability to ambulate unassisted.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three weeks prior to admission, the patient presented with acute urinary retention. Two weeks later (one week before admission), he experienced an influenza-like illness and a transient episode of diplopia. Seven days prior to admission, he developed progressive muscle weakness in both legs, culminating in inability to walk without assistance upon hospital presentation. He reported paresthesias and pain in both legs. Four days post-admission, motor strength showed slight improvement, but areflexia persisted.
subjective.past_medical_history: Episode of acute urinary retention 3 weeks prior to admission; resident of Paramaribo, Suriname.
subjective.review_of_systems: Transient diplopia, paresthesias and pain in bilateral lower extremities; denies sensory level or bowel dysfunction.

objective.physical_examination: At admission: Predominant lower extremity muscle weakness (MRC score 4/5); generalized areflexia in bilateral upper and lower extremities; no sensory level or signs of spinal cord involvement. Four days post-admission: Muscle strength improved (MRC score arms 5/5; legs proximal 5/5, distal 4/5), with persistent areflexia in all four extremities. At discharge (day 7): Unable to walk without assistance.
objective.advanced_workup: MRI scan of the spine (performed 2 weeks prior to weakness onset): No abnormalities, excluding acute myelitis and cauda equina syndrome. Lumbar puncture (day 2 post-admission): Cerebrospinal fluid demonstrated elevated protein (4.4 g/L) and slightly increased cell count (32.7 x 10^6/L). Motor nerve conduction study (NCS) (day 15 post-onset): Severely decreased nerve conduction velocity (NCV) and prolonged distal motor latency (DML) across all tested nerves, with decreased compound muscle action potential (CMAP) predominantly in the lower extremities, consistent with the demyelinating subtype of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy subtype) associated with acute Zika virus infection, confirmed by detection of ZIKV RNA in urine collected on day 2 post-admission (Ct value 35.7). The patient did not receive intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) or plasma exchange due to local unavailability. Managed supportively; at discharge (day 7) he remained unable to ambulate unassisted. At 4-month follow-up, he could walk a few steps without assistance but was unable to live independently or return to work.
